# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide, affecting more than 60 million people [1]. For decades, neurohormonal blockade with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists formed the therapeutic backbone for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The development of sacubitril/valsartan, the first angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift by simultaneously augmenting beneficial natriuretic peptide signaling while inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [4]. Inhibition of neprilysin increases circulating natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of maladaptive cardiac remodeling [5]. Because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, isolated neprilysin inhibition can paradoxically raise angiotensin II levels; thus, concomitant angiotensin receptor blockade with valsartan is essential [6]. Earlier attempts combining neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) were abandoned because of unacceptable angioedema risk attributed to dual bradykinin accumulation [7]. Sacubitril/valsartan was therefore designed as a supramolecular complex avoiding direct ACE inhibition [8].

## Landmark Clinical Trials

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8,442 patients with HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%, later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [9]. The trial was stopped early because of overwhelming benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, with significant reductions in all-cause mortality [9]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progressive pump failure death [10], improvements in quality of life [11], and slowing of renal function decline compared with enalapril [12]. Effects were consistent across the spectrum of disease severity and background therapy [13].

The TITRATION study established that gradual up-titration improved tolerability, particularly in patients not previously on high-dose renin-angiotensin inhibitors [14]. The PIONEER-HF trial extended these findings to hospitalized patients with acute decompensated HFrEF, demonstrating that in-hospital initiation produced greater reductions in NT-proBNP than enalapril with comparable safety [15]. The TRANSITION study similarly supported initiation before or shortly after discharge [16].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial randomized patients with ejection fraction ≥45% to sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan [17]. The primary composite endpoint narrowly missed statistical significance (rate ratio 0.87, P=0.06) [17]. However, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction and in women [18]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF suggested that treatment benefit extends to patients with ejection fraction below normal, supporting use across a broader range [19].

## Biomarker and Reverse Remodeling Effects

The PROVE-HF study showed that sacubitril/valsartan initiation was associated with reductions in NT-proBNP that correlated with favorable cardiac reverse remodeling, including improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction and volumes [20]. The EVALUATE-HF trial demonstrated effects on aortic stiffness and cardiac structure [21]. These mechanistic findings reinforce the disease-modifying potential of ARNI therapy [22].

## Safety and Tolerability

The principal safety concerns are symptomatic hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and angioedema [9]. To minimize angioedema risk, a 36-hour washout is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor [23]. Hypotension was more common with sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril, whereas cough, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment were less frequent [9]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally found ARNI to be economically favorable in HFrEF [24].

## Guidelines and Clinical Implementation

Contemporary guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and the European Society of Cardiology recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy for HFrEF, with a class I recommendation to replace ACE inhibitors or ARBs [25,26]. ARNI is now considered one of the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [27]. Despite robust evidence, real-world uptake remains suboptimal owing to clinical inertia, cost, and tolerability concerns [28].

## Future Directions and Conclusion

Ongoing research is examining ARNI in specific populations including post-myocardial infarction patients (PARADISE-MI), which did not meet its primary endpoint but showed nominal benefit on some outcomes [29]. Other areas of interest include use in advanced HF, right ventricular dysfunction, and combination with newer agents [30]. In summary, sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF, offering mortality and morbidity benefits superior to conventional renin-angiotensin inhibition, with emerging but more nuanced roles in HFpEF. Optimizing implementation and individualizing therapy remain key priorities.
